hypotheses.title: mintAllocatedShares lacks access control allowing theft of allocated shares
hypotheses.description: `mintAllocatedShares(address account, uint256 value)` has no `onlyQueue`/`onlyVaultOrQueue` modifier, unlike `mint()` which is guarded by `onlyVaultOrQueue`. It decrements `$.allocatedShares` and calls `mint(account, value)` — `mint` will then pass its own `onlyVaultOrQueue` check only because `mintAllocatedShares` internally invokes it, but the entrypoint itself is fully public. Any external caller can therefore redirect the vault's accumulated `allocatedShares` pool to an arbitrary `account`.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Wait until `allocatedShares > 0` (normal after deposit reports allocate shares for depositors). 2) As any untrusted EOA, call `mintAllocatedShares(attacker, allocatedShares)`. 3) The function passes the internal `mint` modifier since the call originates from the manager itself, minting shares to the attacker and zeroing the pool. 4) Attacker then redeems/burns those shares via a redeem queue to withdraw real assets.
hypotheses.impact: Direct theft of all currently-allocated-but-unclaimed depositor shares; vault insolvency because pending depositors' claims are wiped while attacker redeems the underlying.
hypotheses.recommendation: Add `onlyQueue` (or `onlyVaultOrQueue`) to `mintAllocatedShares`, restricting callers to registered queues/vault.

hypotheses.title: RiskManager.setVault is callable once by anyone to hijack vault binding
hypotheses.description: `setVault(address)` has no owner/role check; it only enforces `$.vault == address(0)`. Deployment order through `VaultConfigurator` is a single-shot front-runnable window: after `riskManagerFactory.create(...)` deploys the proxy but before `IRiskManager(riskManager).setVault(vault)` runs, any external actor can call `setVault(attacker)` and permanently bind the RiskManager to the attacker's contract. `onlyRole`, `onlyVaultOrRole`, and `onlyQueueOrRole` all read `vault()` from this value, so the checks become self-referential once vault is attacker-controlled.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Watch mempool for `VaultConfigurator.create` which deploys a fresh RiskManager proxy with `$.vault == 0`. 2) Immediately call `riskManager.setVault(attackerEOA)` with higher gas. 3) When the configurator's subsequent `setVault(vault)` call runs, it reverts with `InvalidInitialization` (or is a no-op), leaving attacker as the trusted vault. 4) Attacker, as `vault()`, now passes every `onlyVaultOrRole`/`onlyQueueOrRole` check and can call `modifyVaultBalance`, `modifyPendingAssets`, `modifySubvaultBalance`, `setSubvaultLimit` etc.
hypotheses.impact: Full control over the risk module of a victim's vault (creating subvault limits/balances arbitrarily, fabricating pending/balancing numbers, allowing/disallowing subvault assets), enabling theft through downstream share minting/asset movement.
hypotheses.recommendation: Make `setVault` gated to the factory/configurator (e.g., `onlyOwner` or an immutable factory check) or perform the binding inside `initialize`.

hypotheses.title: Consensus.checkSignatures allows duplicate signers to satisfy threshold
hypotheses.description: `checkSignatures` accepts any nonempty array of size >= `threshold` and does not enforce uniqueness of signer addresses. A single valid signer can be repeated `threshold` times with the same signature, satisfying the threshold as long as the count matches. This defeats the multisig threshold entirely, meaning one compromised/rogue signer's signature is enough to authorize any `Order` presented to a Signature queue.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker obtains one valid EIP712 signature from any single legit signer (e.g., via replayed order, or a colluding signer). 2) Attacker constructs `signatures = [sig, sig, ..., sig]` with length == threshold and passes it to `SignatureDepositQueue.deposit`/`SignatureRedeemQueue.redeem`. 3) `requireValidSignatures` iterates and returns true because each entry has an allowed signer and a valid signature. 4) Attacker's order executes: mints shares at arbitrary price for a deposit, or burns arbitrary shares / drains assets for a redeem.
hypotheses.impact: Full bypass of multisig gating: unauthorized minting, share burning, and asset withdrawal from the vault via Signature queues.
hypotheses.recommendation: Enforce unique signers in `checkSignatures` (e.g., track seen addresses in a bitmap/set) and require strictly distinct signer entries.

hypotheses.title: SignatureQueue order hash omits chainId/contract, enabling cross-chain replay
hypotheses.description: The EIP-712 domain is initialized with only `name_` and `version_` (no `chainId` and no `verifyingContract`), and the `Order` struct itself does not include `chainId` or the queue address. `order.queue` is included in the struct, but the domain separator is identical across all chains and all deployments that share the same name/version. A signature valid on one chain (or one deployment) is therefore valid on any other chain/deployment with the same name/version, as long as the queue address matches.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker observes a valid signed `Order` (with signatures) on chain A for a SignatureDepositQueue/SignatureRedeemQueue. 2) Attacker replays the exact same `Order` and signatures on chain B (or a forked/duplicate deployment) where the same queue address exists and the caller's nonce is still at the same value. 3) `validateOrder` passes because the domain separator is identical and the nonce matches. 4) The order executes again, minting shares or draining assets on the second chain.
hypotheses.impact: Duplicate execution of signed orders across chains/deployments: unauthorized minting of shares or draining of vault assets, breaking accounting and causing loss of funds.
hypotheses.recommendation: Include `block.chainid` and `address(this)` in the EIP-712 domain (or add them to the `Order` struct) so signatures are bound to a specific chain and queue contract.

hypotheses.title: Slots in VaultModule use wrong storage slot name; collides with SubvaultModule
hypotheses.description: `_vaultStorage()` returns the slot computed with name "SubvaultModule" (`_subvaultModuleStorageSlot` is set via `SlotLibrary.getSlot("SubvaultModule", name_, version_)`) instead of "VaultModule". The `Vault` contract inherits both `VaultModule` (which stores `riskManager` and `subvaults`) and `SubvaultModule` (which stores `vault`). Because both use the same derived slot, `riskManager`/`subvaults` and `vault` overlap in storage and overwrite each other.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1. Any deployment of `Vault` will have `subvaults`/`riskManager` stored in the same slot as `vault`. 2. Calls that read `vault()` (e.g. `ShareManager.updateChecks` via `_shareManagerStorage().vault`) or `riskManager()` will read garbage/incorrect addresses. 3. An untrusted user can call functions that depend on `vault()`/`riskManager()` (e.g. `CallModule.call`, `hookPullAssets`, `pullAssets`) to hit corrupted state and trigger unauthorized behaviours or reverts, since the check `caller == vault()` compares against a colliding value.
hypotheses.impact: Corrupted vault state; the vault contract reads a wrong `vault`/`riskManager` address, allowing `CallModule.call` and `*Assets` flows to operate with broken authority checks; system becomes unusable after initialization and risk of unauthorized asset movement if the collided values accidentally match attacker-controlled addresses.
hypotheses.recommendation: Use the correct slot name: `_riskManagerStorageSlot = SlotLibrary.getSlot("VaultModule", name_, version_)` (or distinct string) for `VaultModule` so the storage layout does not collide with `SubvaultModule`.

hypotheses.title: claimShares(account) lets anyone push accumulated shares to any account
hypotheses.description: `claimShares(address account)` is external with no access control and loops all deposit queues calling `IDepositQueue(queue).claim(account)`. Because `DepositQueue._claim` uses `$.requestOf[account]` and mints to `account`, a third party can force any arbitrary account's pending deposit to be claimed. While accounting stays correct, it bypasses the intended "user claims their own shares" flow and can be used for griefing (e.g., front-running a report to trigger mint/fee interactions) or as a reentrancy/DoS lever against the account.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Victim has a pending deposit in a deposit queue. 2) Attacker calls `ShareModule.claimShares(victim)`. 3) All deposit queues execute `_claim(victim)`, minting to victim and deleting their `requestOf` entry. 4) Attacker can repeat every block to interfere with any victim-driven sequence, or couple with `TokenizedShareManager._update`'s `claimShares` to force additional state transitions during transfers.
hypotheses.impact: Unauthorized state transition on a victim's account; lockup/lockup-flag bypass (mint path passes through `updateChecks` for the victim), and potential DoS/griefing for integrations expecting claim-on-own-behalf semantics.
hypotheses.recommendation: Restrict `claimShares` so callers can only claim for `_msgSender()` (or restrict to trusted roles); avoid an arbitrary-account parameter with no caller check.

hypotheses.title: SignatureDepositQueue mints requested shares without verifying price against ordered assets
hypotheses.description: `deposit()` validates the order via `validateOrder`, which checks the oracle price only if an oracle is set. If `oracle_ == address(0)`, no price validation occurs, and the queue mints `order.requested` shares for `order.ordered` assets. The `requested` amount is entirely signer-controlled. A malicious or compromised signer (or a user who obtains valid signatures) can set `requested` arbitrarily high relative to `ordered`, minting far more shares than the deposited assets are worth, diluting existing shareholders.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker obtains a valid signed order (or is a signer) with `ordered = 1 wei` and `requested = 1e30`. 2) Calls `deposit()`. 3) `validateOrder` passes (no oracle check if oracle is zero, or oracle check passes if price is within bounds). 4) `mint(order.recipient, order.requested)` mints 1e30 shares for 1 wei of assets. 5) Attacker redeems shares for a large portion of vault assets.
hypotheses.impact: Massive dilution of existing shareholders; theft of vault assets via over-minting.
hypotheses.recommendation: Require oracle to be set and always validate the implied price against the oracle, or enforce a maximum ratio between `requested` and `ordered`.

hypotheses.title: SignatureQueue price validation uses inverted ratio for redeem queues
hypotheses.description: For deposit queues the code computes `priceD18 = requested/ordered` (shares per asset), but for redeem queues it computes `priceD18 = ordered/requested` (assets per share) with Ceil rounding. The oracle's `validatePrice` compares this against the stored report price which is denominated as shares-per-asset (used in DepositQueue `_handleReport` as `shares = assets * priceD18 / 1e18`). For redeem queues the ratio is inverted, so a legitimate order will be rejected or, worse, an attacker can craft an order whose inverted ratio happens to fall within the deviation band while the actual economic exchange rate is far off, letting them mint/burn shares at a manipulated rate.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker observes oracle report price P (shares per asset). 2) Submits a redeem order with `ordered` (shares) and `requested` (assets) chosen so that `ordered/requested ≈ P` (i.e. the inverted ratio matches P) rather than `requested/ordered ≈ P`. 3) `validatePrice` passes because the inverted ratio is within deviation bounds. 4) Attacker burns far fewer shares than the assets they receive (or vice versa), extracting value from the vault.
hypotheses.impact: Redeemers can burn fewer shares than the fair amount for the assets they withdraw, draining the vault; or legitimate redeemers are blocked. Direct loss of funds / insolvency.
hypotheses.recommendation: Use the same orientation as the oracle report for both queue types (e.g. always `requested/ordered` for shares-per-asset, or invert consistently), and remove the Ceil rounding asymmetry.

hypotheses.title: ShareModule.createQueue lets role-holder create queue with attacker-chosen owner
hypotheses.description: `createQueue(version, isDeposit, owner, asset, data)` accepts an arbitrary `owner` for the new queue's TransparentUpgradeableProxy. The factory's `create` uses `owner` as the proxy admin. If `CREATE_QUEUE_ROLE` is delegated broadly (or the holder's key is compromised), the queue admin can later upgrade the queue to a malicious implementation stealing assets it holds. This is a privilege-abuse surface inherent to hot-key role holders rather than a pure external-actor exploit.
hypotheses.attackPath: A role holder (or compromised key) calls `createQueue` with `owner = attacker`; later, the attacker (as proxy admin) upgrades the queue implementation and drains funds sent to it by users.
hypotheses.impact: Loss of user assets routed into the queue if a role-holder key is compromised; queue-owner privileges mismatched with intended governance.
hypotheses.recommendation: Force `owner` to be a governance-controlled address (e.g., `address(this)` / vault admin) instead of accepting an arbitrary parameter, or restrict to a dedicated role.

hypotheses.title: RedeemQueue claim uses stale batch.shares causing over/under payout
hypotheses.description: In `claim()`, the payout is computed as `Math.mulDiv(shares, batch.assets, batch.shares)` and then `batch.assets -= assets_` and `batch.shares -= shares`. However, `batch.shares` is the total shares for the batch, and multiple users can claim against the same batch. The math is correct per-claim, but the batch's `assets` was computed at report time using `Math.mulDiv(shares, 1 ether, priceD18)` which floors. When many small claims occur, each `mulDiv` floors independently, so the sum of individual payouts can be less than `batch.assets`, leaving dust stranded in the batch that is never claimable (since `batch.shares` reaches 0 but `batch.assets` may remain > 0). Conversely, if the last claimer takes the remainder, earlier claimers were underpaid relative to their pro-rata share.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker splits a large redeem into many tiny redeem requests across many accounts/timestamps. 2) Each claim floors the payout. 3) Attacker (or any user) observes that the sum of floors < batch.assets, leaving stranded assets. 4) The stranded assets remain in the queue contract and are not attributable to any shares, effectively locking funds or allowing the last claimer to sweep them.
hypotheses.impact: Stranded assets in the RedeemQueue contract; some redeemers receive less than their pro-rata share; funds effectively frozen or misallocated.
hypotheses.recommendation: Track remaining assets/shares and pay the last claimer the residual `batch.assets` when `batch.shares` reaches zero, or use a cumulative accounting scheme that preserves the invariant sum(payouts) == batch.assets.

hypotheses.title: SignatureQueue validateOrder accepts zero/absent oracle report as valid
hypotheses.description: `oracle_.validatePrice(priceD18, order.asset)` returns `(true, true)` when `prevPriceD18 == 0` (first report) and `(false, false)` only for unsupported assets. The check `if (!isValid || isSuspicious) revert` therefore reverts on the first report (isSuspicious=true) — but more importantly, if the oracle has never reported for the asset, `report.priceD18 == 0` and `_validatePrice` returns `(true, true)`, which reverts. However, if the asset was added to supported assets but never reported, `validatePrice` returns `(true, true)` → revert. The real flaw: there is no check that the report is fresh (timestamp). A stale report (e.g. from months ago) is accepted as long as the price is within deviation, so signed orders can execute at an outdated price.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Oracle stops updating (or updates infrequently). 2) Attacker waits until market price diverges significantly from the last reported price. 3) Attacker obtains a signed order (or is the signer's counterparty) at the stale price and executes deposit/redeem, receiving shares/assets at the outdated rate. 4) Attacker immediately redeems/deposits at the true market rate elsewhere, capturing the difference.
hypotheses.impact: Value extraction from the vault at stale prices; existing holders diluted.
hypotheses.recommendation: In `validateOrder`, also require `report.timestamp` to be within an acceptable freshness window (e.g. `block.timestamp - report.timestamp <= maxAge`), and reject zero-price reports explicitly.

hypotheses.title: SignatureRedeemQueue.redeem burns shares before hook pulls assets, enabling reentrancy
hypotheses.description: In `redeem()`, the queue burns the recipient's shares, then calls `vault_.callHook(order.requested)` which delegates to a redeem hook (e.g. `BasicRedeemHook`) that pulls assets from subvaults via `hookPullAssets`. The hook is an external call that can re-enter the queue or vault before `modifyVaultBalance` and `sendAssets` complete, and the nonReentrant guard only protects the queue itself, not the vault/hook path. Because state (burn, hook pull) is interleaved with external calls, an attacker controlling a hook or subvault can observe inconsistent state.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker registers a malicious redeem hook (or controls a subvault whose `pullAssets` re-enters). 2) Calls `redeem()` with a signed order. 3) During `callHook`, the hook re-enters `SignatureRedeemQueue.redeem()` or `ShareModule.callHook`/`getLiquidAssets` while shares are already burned but vault balance not yet decremented. 4) Attacker drains assets or double-counts liquid assets.
hypotheses.impact: Loss of vault funds / incorrect accounting of liquid assets and vault balance.
hypotheses.recommendation: Perform all state updates (burn, balance modification) before external hook calls, or add a vault-level reentrancy guard covering the hook path.

hypotheses.title: SignatureDepositQueue.deposit mints shares after external hook call
hypotheses.description: `deposit()` transfers assets to the vault, then calls `vault_.callHook(order.ordered)` (external delegatecall into a deposit hook such as `RedirectingDepositHook`/`LidoDepositHook`), and only afterwards calls `riskManager().modifyVaultBalance` and `shareManager().mint`. The hook can push assets into subvaults and re-enter the vault/queue before shares are minted and before the risk manager balance is updated, allowing state to be read mid-flight.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker submits a signed deposit order. 2) During `callHook`, a malicious hook/subvault re-enters `ShareModule.claimShares`, `getLiquidAssets`, or another queue's `redeem`/`claim` while the vault balance and share supply are stale. 3) Attacker extracts value from the inconsistent state (e.g. redeems at pre-mint price).
hypotheses.impact: Wrong share accounting, potential theft of vault assets.
hypotheses.recommendation: Update risk manager balance and mint shares before invoking the hook, or guard the entire vault flow with a shared reentrancy lock.

hypotheses.title: ShareModule.claimShares loops all queues; one reverting queue bricks claims
hypotheses.description: `claimShares(account)` iterates over every asset and every queue and calls `IDepositQueue(queue).claim(account)` for each deposit queue. If any single deposit queue's `claim` reverts (e.g., a queue whose `mintAllocatedShares` reverts due to insufficient allocated shares, or a paused/broken queue), the entire loop reverts, so the user cannot claim shares from any other queue. Since `TokenizedShareManager._update` calls `claimShares(from)` and `claimShares(to)` on every transfer/mint/burn, a single broken deposit queue bricks all share transfers for that account.
hypotheses.attackPath: An attacker can create conditions where a deposit queue's `claim` reverts for a victim (e.g., by ensuring `allocatedShares` is insufficient via queue interactions), then any transfer involving the victim reverts, freezing their shares. Even without an attacker, a single misbehaving queue freezes all users' share movements.
hypotheses.impact: Frozen shares / DoS on all share transfers and claims for affected accounts.
hypotheses.recommendation: Wrap each queue claim in try/catch, or make `claim` non-reverting and skip failures, so one queue cannot block others.

hypotheses.title: SignatureQueue nonce is per-caller and not bound to order fields, enabling replay of distinct orders
hypotheses.description: The nonce is stored per `order.caller` and incremented after each execution, but the nonce is not bound to the specific order contents beyond being part of the signed hash. Because `order.caller` must equal `_msgSender()`, an attacker cannot directly replay another user's order. However, the nonce is a simple counter with no per-order uniqueness guarantee: if a signer signs two different orders with the same nonce (e.g., due to off-chain race or reuse), only the first executes and the second is permanently blocked, and conversely a signed order can be replayed by the caller until the nonce increments. More importantly, the nonce is not tied to a deadline/orderId uniqueness, so a signed order remains valid indefinitely until the caller's nonce advances.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) A signer signs an `Order` for caller C with nonce N. 2) C does not execute it immediately. 3) The signed order remains valid as long as C's nonce is N and `order.deadline` has not passed. 4) C (or anyone who obtains the signed order) can execute it at any later time within the deadline, potentially after market conditions change, front-running other users.
hypotheses.impact: Stale signed orders can be executed at a later, more favorable time, causing price/accounting discrepancies and potential loss to the vault or other users.
hypotheses.recommendation: Bind the nonce to the order (e.g., include `orderId` in the nonce derivation) and/or enforce a short deadline; consider invalidating the nonce on any state change that affects the order.
